issues.title: multi-language prompt injection detection
issues.body:
all current prompt injection rules match English-only phrases, which is fine for v1. prompt injection attacks are known to succeed against LLMs using non-English equivalents though

warlock rules today would miss:
- `ignora las instrucciones anteriores` (Spanish for "ignore previous instructions")
- `игнорируй предыдущие инструкции` (Russian)
- `忽略之前的指令` (Chinese)
- variants across ~10 common attack-target languages

this is a known gap across a lot of security scanners for LLMs/context

## proposal

1. research top 10 most-attacked languages for LLM injection (OWASP LLM Lit, Anthropic and OpenAI red-team write-ups)
2. for each of the 5 prompt injection rules, add translated variants as additional YARA strings
3. add negative test cases using ordinary non-English text to verify no false positive on legitimate content in those languages

we can't detect ALL languages, but we can be better

issues.title: Replace #63 stopgap in posthog_feature_attack (tighten TP shape) + consumers must not block trusted first-party skills untriaged
issues.body:
## Summary

Two separate problems surfaced when `prompt_injection_posthog_feature_attack` blocked a first-party skill install. [#63](https://github.com/PostHog/warlock/pull/63) (shipped in 0.2.4) was a stopgap aimed at one phrasing; it does not resolve either root cause. This issue tracks both.

## Problem 1 — the rule over-fires on non-instruction framing (rule-level)

The rule matches a verb + feature substring (`disable autocapture`) anywhere, regardless of the surrounding grammar. That catches informational and even *anti*-injection prose. Two real first-party shapes trip it:

1. **Permissive-modal config docs** — "You can disable autocapture entirely by setting `autocapture` to `false`." (#63's `$benign_config_doc` guard suppresses this one.)
2. **Negated / prohibitive guidance** — "Do not disable autocapture, do not disable session recording." This is guidance to *keep* the feature on, but the rule matches the `disable autocapture` substring. **#63 does not cover this — it still fires.**

#63's guard is also a whole-buffer negative match (`any of ($attack_*) and not $benign_config_doc`): because a bare string in the condition is true if it matches anywhere, any content containing the benign phrase suppresses the entire rule. A real injection can append a benign-shaped clause to evade. It also pushes consumer-context judgment into the engine.

### Proposed direction (rule)

Replace the negative guard with a tightened true-positive shape: require actual instruction framing so neither permissive-modal ("you can disable X") nor negated ("do not disable X") prose matches, while bare imperatives ("Disable X.") still do.

**Constraint:** yara-x's regex engine (Rust-based) is not expected to support lookbehind/lookahead — confirm during implementation. If so, "match `disable X` unless preceded by `you can` / `do not`" can't be expressed directly; use an imperative/clause-boundary lead-in instead.

## Problem 2 — a consumer can hard-block trusted first-party skills (the bigger half)

Warlock only detects; consumers decide what a match means. A consumer's skill-install scan currently **terminates on a match without the false-positive triage pass that other scan paths use**, so any benign match on trusted first-party skill content blocks the install. Tightening the rule (Problem 1) reduces the noise but does not fix this — the next benign match on any skill re-triggers it. **The guarantee that first-party skills don't get blocked lives in the consumer wiring, not the rule.**

The consumer-side fix (ensure the install path triages, and/or treat genuinely first-party skills by provenance) is tracked and PR'd in the consumer repo. Design constraint carried there: a trusted-source bypass must key off genuine first-party provenance, not a loose path pattern, or a real injection planted at that path would go unscanned.

## Acceptance criteria

**Rule (this repo):**
- The `not $benign_config_doc` guard from #63 is removed.
- Neither permissive-modal nor negated/prohibitive config prose matches; bare imperatives and existing positive cases still match.
- No single string can suppress the whole rule across the buffer.
- The false-positive shapes above are locked in as negative-match tests.

**Consumer (tracked in the consumer repo, noted here for context):**
- A benign match on trusted first-party skill content does not hard-block/terminate the install without triage.
- Any trusted-source bypass keys off first-party provenance, not a loose path pattern.

## References

- PR #63 — the 0.2.4 stopgap being replaced.

issues.title: Make warlock integration harness-agnostic: per-run scanner instance + streaming results
issues.body:
## Problem

warlock's **core** is already portable — `scan(content) -> matches` is a pure, stateless engine that drops into any project. But the **reporting/telemetry lifecycle** currently has to be wired by each integrator, and the wizard's integration (`src/lib/yara-hooks.ts`) reveals why that's fragile:

- It accumulates scan results into a **module-level singleton** (`scanViolations` array) and flushes once at "the end" of a run, then resets.
- This has two portability defects:
  1. **It needs an "end."** Accumulate-then-flush-once forces every harness to define and correctly hook "the run is over." Miss it and reporting silently never fires.
  2. **It's a singleton.** One shared buffer per process silently assumes *one sequential run*. It breaks under: parallel/fan-out harnesses (runs clobber each other), long-running daemons (never "ends"), and serverless (no shared module state).

The wizard just hit this concretely: when its runner was split into multiple harnesses (linear + experimental orchestrator), the report flush — bolted into one exit path — would silently not fire for the other harness. The current stopgap is an idempotent `flushScanReport()` finalizer wired at the wizard's single dispatcher seam, but that's wizard-internal glue; it doesn't port to a different harness shape.

## Goal

Anyone should be able to hook warlock into any project — whatever their harness shape — with ≤1 line of integration code and no knowledge of warlock's reporting lifecycle.

## Proposed shape

The root cause of both defects is **batching into a singleton**. Remove the batch and both evaporate. Offer two complementary triggers so no harness lifecycle has to be reasoned about:

1. **Push (streaming) — removes the "end" problem entirely.** A per-run scanner emits each match to a consumer-supplied sink as it happens:
   ```ts
   const scanner = warlock.createScanner({ rules, onMatch: m => sink.send(m) });
   ```
   No buffer, no "end" — daemon, serverless, and parallel fan-out are all identical.

2. **Per-run instance + dispose — for consumers who still want one aggregated summary.** The buffer moves off the module singleton and into a scanner instance, flushed on dispose (scope-bound, concurrency-safe):
   ```ts
   await using scanner = warlock.createScanner({ rules });   // owns its own results
   // ... summary auto-emitted at scope exit, or scanner.report() on demand
   ```

Between push (no end needed) and dispose (scope-bound end), virtually every harness is covered with ≤1 line; the exotic case falls back to explicit `scanner.close()`.

## Layering (respects warlock's engine-only philosophy)

| Layer | Owns | Ports? |
|---|---|---|
| warlock core | `scan -> matches` (pure) | anywhere, already |
| thin optional adapter | per-run scanner instance: streaming `onMatch` + disposable summary | anywhere — no harness assumptions |
| integrator glue | maps the adapter onto *this* harness's hooks | tiny, per-project |

The consumer still decides *how to respond* to matches (warlock stays engine-only); this just stops every integrator from re-implementing accumulation + lifecycle.

## Acceptance

- No module-level singleton state in the reporting path.
- A new integrator can wire warlock into a fresh project's harness (any shape) with ≤1 line and no lifecycle knowledge.
- Concurrent/parallel runs don't share or clobber scan state.

Context: surfaced while integrating warlock into the PostHog wizard (PostHog/wizard, yara-improvements branch).

issues.title: Add INTEGRATING.md guide for consumers
issues.body:
## Problem

The Warlock skill (`.claude/skills/warlock`) references an `INTEGRATING.md` — *"guide for engineers integrating the Warlock into a consumer application; update this when changing the public API"* — but the file doesn't actually exist. The repo only has `README.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

Right now the README doubles as both the charter/design doc *and* the de-facto integration reference. That works, but there's no single place that walks a consumer (context-mill, and future ones) through wiring the Warlock in end to end.

## What it should cover

- Installing the Warlock as a dependency (incl. the `git+https://...` install pattern context-mill currently uses, and how to refresh it)
- Minimal `scan()` usage + reading `ScanMatch` (`rule`, `metadata`, `matchedStrings`)
- Opt-in `triageMatches()` usage: providing an LLM callback, batching/truncation behavior, the fail-safe-to-`true_positive` contract
- Which parts of the API are stable vs. which evolve (rule names are not API; categories/severities are)
- A note that consumers decide actions — the Warlock only detects

## Why the Warlock is the right home

Integration guidance for the Warlock's public API belongs next to the API it documents, so it stays in sync when the API changes. Putting it in a consumer repo would drift and wouldn't serve future consumers equally.

## Context

Surfaced while adding the `matchedStrings` field to `ScanMatch` — updating the docs revealed the referenced `INTEGRATING.md` was never created.

issues.title: Make LLM triage deterministic + plug-and-play (rules-only engine, provider adapters, sane defaults)
issues.body:
## The problem

The warlock's LLM triage step is non-deterministic, and it bit a consumer for real. A context-mill CI build flipped from failing (64 "threats") to passing on a plain re-run, with zero code changes. Same files, same rules, same warlock version. The only thing that changed was the triage model's verdict.

Two root causes:

1. **The triage prompt never tells the model what actually matched.** We hand it the whole file plus the rule name, but not the specific substring the YARA rule fired on (`engine.ts` drops the offsets). So the model hunts through the file and sometimes blames the wrong text. In our case the real trigger was a harmless `You are now logged in` greeting in a demo app, but the model sometimes pinned it on an unrelated `You are an audit subagent` line and called it a role hijack.
2. **Temperature isn't pinned.** Triage runs at the model's default temperature, so the same question can get different answers run to run. For a blocking security gate we want the same answer every time.

The wrinkle: the warlock does not make the LLM call, the consumer does (bring-your-own-provider). So today every consumer has to remember to set temperature 0 themselves, which is exactly how one consumer ends up silently flaky.

## What we want

Keep the warlock a **rules-only engine** (it should not hold credentials or make network calls), but give consumers a plug-and-play, hard-to-misconfigure setup with good defaults baked in:

1. **Pass the matched substring(s) through to triage.** yara-x already returns `patterns[].matches[].{offset, length}` per match; we currently throw them away in `engine.ts`. Capture them (slice the byte payload, not the JS string, so multi-byte chars stay aligned), add them to `ScanMatch`, and include them in the triage prompt so the model judges the actual trigger instead of guessing. Cap count and length so prompts stay sane.
2. **Centralize the recommended settings (temperature 0, etc.) in the warlock, applied via plug-and-play adapters.** The warlock still calls nothing itself, but ships:
   - a clear provider contract,
   - optional thin adapters for common LLMs (wrap a consumer's existing Anthropic / OpenAI client) that apply the recommended defaults automatically, so nobody has to remember temperature 0,
   - a single config object with suggested defaults that consumers override only when they need to.
3. **Optional: a real setup step** like `npx warlock init` that scaffolds the wiring for a consumer (the "wizard"), run on purpose after install, not hidden install-script magic.

## Why this matters

A security gate that flips pass/fail at random trains people to just hit re-run until it goes green, which defeats the whole point of the gate. Making triage deterministic and the setup plug-and-play fixes both the reliability and the DX.

## Out of scope / notes

- The immediate flaky build in context-mill is being handled separately as a smaller fix. This issue is the durable architecture work.
- The adapters must not turn the warlock into the credential-holder or hard-depend on any specific LLM SDK.

## Context
From Vincent's review on PR #14 — the current hardcoded secret rules cover AWS, GitHub PAT, and Stripe live keys. There are many more secret formats worth detecting.

## Reference projects to pull patterns from
- **TruffleHog**: https://github.com/trufflesecurity/trufflehog/tree/main/pkg/detectors

## High-value candidates to add next
- Slack tokens (`xoxb-`, `xoxp-`, `xoxs-`)
- Twilio keys (`SK` + 32 hex)
- SendGrid keys (`SG.`)
- Database connection strings (postgres://, mongodb://, mysql://)

issues.title: Redesign: should agents be allowed to git push at all?
issues.body:
## Context
From Vincent's review on PR #13 — the current `exfiltration_git_push_non_origin` rule only blocks pushes to non-origin remotes. Vincent raises three points:

1. **Maybe agents should never push at all.** There may not be a legitimate reason for an AI agent to push code.
2. **"origin" is just a convention.** Many developers working on forks call their remote "upstream" or something else. Filtering on the word "origin" isn't reliable.
3. **Force pushes should be treated differently.** A force push is more destructive and should be split into its own severity level.

## Discussion needed
- Is "block all pushes" too aggressive? Some agent workflows (auto-PR creation) do need to push.
- Should we switch to an allow-list model (block all pushes EXCEPT to allow-listed remotes)?
- How to handle force pushes — separate rule or higher severity within the same rule?

Previously: #512

I'm changing how I think about goals this quarter. Supporting the products I'm responsible for is my default goal and should be treated as BAU -- I won't spell out every item, just the tent-pole activities that need special coordination or focus. My actual goal sits outside the products I work on but still needs extra attention, and the product work takes the slot that would normally be my sidequest.

#### PostHog MCP

#### Marketing for agents

Work that makes PostHog and its tools visible to agents, or broadens the product set they can reach.

- [x] [Point MCP agents at the changelog for recently shipped features](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/77334)

- [x] [Surface related skills to MCP proactively](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/pull/78433)
---

### Things I care about this quarter

In [The Numbers Game](https://www.amazon.co.uk/dp/0241963621?psc=1&smid=A3P5ROKL5A1OLE&ref_=chk_typ_imgToDp) they split sports into strong-link and weak-link. In strong-link games like basketball one great player can win the whole game, so you invest in your best. In weak-link games like football your worst player on the pitch sets your ceiling, so you raise the floor. ([More on this idea applied elsewhere](https://www.pushkin.fm/podcasts/revisionist-history/my-little-hundred-million).)

This has been framing a lot of how I think about marketing at PostHog, because we're both at once.

Nurture flows, for example, are a weak-link activity. If data isn't flowing well internally, for example, then we end up letting things like activation criteria rot and that throws the entire downstream flow into inefficiency. 

Announcements, on the other hand, are a strong-link activity. We do well here by letting one person do their best work and writing a great piece.

With this in mind, **I want to focus this quarter on the weak-link activities** - especially in regard to team organization, PostHog for Startups, and our long-running nurture flows. 

This isn't very glamourous work -- even in the last week I've been told that this can be seen as just "Joe fiddling with emails" -- but I can definitively prove the value and I'm the best person to work on it because I have the most historic context. Strong-link tasks where I can be effective right now are also mostly BAU things anyway: providing feedback, setting context, doing IC work, and hiring.

Team organization feels like an especially important one this quarter. I was a solo PMM for a long time and that meant PMM was a strong-link activity. This carried into how we grew the team -- a PMM per tool, empowered to ship solo as a strong-link. That now conflicts with the new structure because stories will have to be told across multiple surfaces and multiple PMMs. PMM is thereby becoming a weak-link structure and I need to focus more on how we work together in that situation. 

---

### Things I don't care about this quarter

This is defined by priorities: we need to go fast and that will mean ignoring some painpoints.

- **Users briefly confused by the repositioning.** We're changing how we describe ourselves, and some people will be thrown because we no longer sound like the thing they signed up for. That's the cost of repositioning, not a bug to chase -- chasing it would mean hedging, over-clarifying, and thwarting our own positioning.

- **Bespoke support for every tool team.** PMM now operates across products (interfaces), not tools (features), around the self-driving story. If a tool team wants marketing for something that doesn't fit that story, the default answer is no -- not because it doesn't matter, but because it isn't the story we need to tell right now. The machine is the other half of this: teams that want to launch can self-serve through it. We're removing the need for bespoke support, not the ability to launch well.

issues.title: RFC: PostHog for Students
issues.body:
# PostHog for Students

I spoke late last week with a student involved in AggieWorks at UC Davis, who wanted to get on the startups plan. It led me to thinking about a PostHog for Students program. This RFC is the output of that thinking, but it is less of a formal RFC and more of a thoughtblob. 

I'm not looking for a decision off the back of this -- I'm looking to explain my take on the approach that I think offers the most value so that specifically @Zaltsman and @kliment-slice can decide what they want to do, if anything. Some elements of this are definitely a little fuzzy and will rely on them to figure out the details. 

## Why build a student program?

I'll keep this brief because I think it should be straightforward.

**The case for:**

- **Builders of tomorrow.** It sounds cliche, but it's true. Getting in early with these users now can help us build recognition that will last a long time and which will be amplified by network effects.
- **This is very PostHoggy.** PostHog has grown through word of mouth and excels at scrappy-but-ambitious marketing. It's hard to get more grassroots than a college campus.
- **We've got most of the ingredients.** Events, content, merch, and brand. We do each of these things well and we've got a brand people actually want to connect with.
- **It's an unalloyed good.** I'm an old wannabe punk. I think supporting the next generation is a good thing and that the opportunity to do good things is its own reward. Fight me. 

**The case against:**

- **This sounds like hard work.** Building in-roads from the outside takes real investment and we should expect to do most of the heavy lifting.
- **Delayed returns.** As Daniel said, anything we start here we should be comfortable not seeing the results of for 4-5 years.
- **Who drives it?** Anything we do here needs continuing attention. I don't have the capacity to get something off the ground without dropping something else -- but more on that below.

## What users think this could look like

Samar, a student at UC Davis, put together a proposal based on his own research and interviews with students there. Full credit to him -- it's a well-reasoned pitch and helped me think through this properly. [I've shared it here](https://posthog.slack.com/archives/C0AB78YBCNA/p1773397200771009?thread_ts=1773078907.648979&cid=C0AB78YBCNA), internally only due to it containing some user names. 

His diagnosis is that the core problem is education: students don't understand the importance of analytics and aren't getting enough value from PostHog. His proposed solution is a structured ambassador program -- monthly workshops, a resource hub, dedicated support channels. This would focus on educating and building recognition with students, while we'd benefit from the WOM and an open source contribution pipeline.

It's a really great pitch for a standard student ambassador program, but I see things a little differently. 

## Why I see it differently

Two reasons. 

First: PostHog isn't the type of place where we do "standard" things in a well-trod mold. 
Second: I think the solution is solving a problem that's about to disappear.

To me, Samar's research actually reveals isn't that students don't know how to use PostHog. It's that they don't know what questions to ask. 

Jake, for example, doesn't actually want better docs that explain how to use PostHog. He wants direct access to @annaszell to help him ask the right questions. Andrew's teams have sparse dashboards not because they can't use PostHog, but because they're not sure what they're trying to do with the data. 

That's a much more interesting problem to solve. And it's one that's going to get more important, not less, as AI changes how products get built. Instrumenting events and using analytics is getting easier every month. PostHog Wizard already sets up instrumentation in under 90 seconds. PostHog AI already answers data questions in plain English. PostHog Code is going to push this further. The manual, technical work of setting up analytics is being automated away. 

There's no point in teaching students how to use analytics, because we're actively making that obsolete. Instead, what we can uniquely teach them is something different -- and something that doesn't get automated away. How to think like a product builder. How to ask the right questions. How to use data to make decisions rather than just collect it. How to exercise taste when working with AI to build the right things. 

That's PostHog's real edge and it's not something any other analytics company can credibly offer.

## What I'm proposing

A pilot centered on a hackathon at UC Davis, working in partnership with AggieWorks and the student groups Samar has already connected us with.

**The format:**

Students bring whatever they're building -- or build something new, because it's fast enough to do that now with AI. They implement PostHog, get access to PostHog Code (more on that below), and spend the day building and improving. There are structured testing sessions where teams try each other's products and the data from those sessions goes straight into PostHog. Then comes the part I think is most valuable: teams work with PostHog people to interrogate that data, ask better questions, and figure out what to build next.

The education isn't a seminar. It's a live product decision made with real data in front of you, with someone who does this every day sitting next to you.

**Who comes from PostHog:**

Not engineers explaining the importance of analytics. Product managers, and builders who can talk about how to think about products and how PostHog makes these decisions. The opportunity to spend a day building alongside the people who actually built PostHog is a draw that no workshop format can replicate.

**What students get:**

- Access to all PostHog tools including PostHog Code beta
- Merch
- $50,000 PostHog for Students credits for a year (essentially the same as PostHog for Startups, but it comes with this event as a benefit)
- The opportunity to connect directly with PostHog teams and get real feedback on what they're building

**What PostHog gets:**

- Real signal on PostHog Code from a group of engaged, curious builders who will tell us exactly what's wrong with it
- A cohort of students who understand how PostHog thinks, not just how PostHog works
- A talent pipeline that's opt-in and self-selecting

**On logistics:**

Kliment on the events team is already interested in this and has been in conversation with Samar. My proposal is that the events team owns the logistics and scopes out what the investment looks like and if we go ahead. 

## The hard question I'm asking myself

The thing I find most exciting about this -- connecting students with how PostHog actually thinks about building products -- is also the hardest thing to deliver. "Ask better questions" is not a curriculum. How do you make that tangible in a single day?

I think the answer is the testing sessions. The moment where a team sits down with real data about how strangers actually used their product, and has to decide what to do with it -- that's the moment where the abstract becomes concrete. I'd build the whole day around that and work backwards. 

## Should we do this?

I think it's worth testing, but it's ultimately on the Events team to make that decision. IMO We don't need to think about scaling to other campuses or other years right now -- we can make that call when we see what this produces.

The bar for success is simple: are these students genuinely engaged? Do they leave having built something better than they arrived with? Do they stay in touch? If yes, we figure out what comes next. If no, we learned something.

issues.body:
## Request for comments: PostHog Art Show 

We’ve been talking about the art show for a long time, so
idea: A small art gallery where all pieces are PostHog-inspired. Not in a “corporate brand showcase” way, but in a “what does PostHog look like through different people’s lenses” way. or a bunch of different hoggies that we already have

Think illustrations, paintings, prints, weird stuff, maybe even objects. Some serious, some not so much.
This is not tied to a specific launch (yet?), but feels like a strong candidate for a standalone brand + community moment.

### **Why**
- It’s very PostHog-y 
- Involves people across the company + community

issues.title: OST session - community questions and engagement
issues.body:
## Motivation

With our cool brand, we have lots of people who are interested in engaging with us. This could be to ask product and non product related questions, share ideas and feedback, or to connect with other PostHog users. We don't really know what to do with them.

## The topics

There are loosely three topics we discussed: 
- What do we do about the unanswered community questions about PostHog (the product)?
- How do we participate in general discussions about PostHog (the team and company)?
- Synchronous ways to engage with the community, which could mean live streams, online events, office hours.

## 1. Unanswered community questions

### What happens right now
- Some of this on the forum is a support function.
- The community forum has active PostHog users that participate and respond to questions
- Docs has many unanswered questions, practically no active users that respond.
- Unanswered questions look bad

### Open ended questions/proposals
- Should individual product teams own docs questions for their product?
  - How many questions per team do we receive a month?
  - How do we make it convenient to find/sort through them
  - Alerts/notifications?
- Should we opt for mostly community champions/active community members to help us with questions?
- If we do try a community program, how do we do it? What's a PostHog way to do these.

### Action items
- Get data on community questions.
  - How many?
  - Who responds to them?
  - Are they in docs or in forum?
  - Break downs by page and product
- Find the active community members
- Ship Karma and badges
- We will not do loose community engagement through things like Discord, we should discuss **synchronous engagement** like streams/office hours. 


## 2. Non-support questions and discussions

### What happens right now
We occasionally participate. We also shitpost from different accounts on socials

### Things we want to try
- Use Reddit more
- Throw fun #no-context-posthog, weird discussions, new hoggies, weird content ideas, all the cool stuff in #do-more-weird on Reddit and forums. See if this helps with community engagement.

## 3. Synchronous stuff

### What happens rn?

Nothing.

### What could we do?
- Streamed demos
- Q & A
- Rotating through each team weekly, give live demo, followed by Q&A with chat
- Have a few floaters to answer/curate questions from chat.

### Why we like synchronous engagement
- Time boxed, have our full attention, high communication bandwidth to engage with individuals.
- Feels special
- Reuse for video content
- Great for real, serious convos.

issues.title: information_schema compat: `NULL AS udt_schema` is INTEGER-typed, so filtering it against a string errors — breaks Metabase column sync
issues.body:
## Problem

`information_schema.columns` is rewritten to `main.information_schema_columns_compat` (`transpiler/transform/information_schema.go`), and all three definitions of that view declare the UDT columns as bare, untyped `NULL`:

| Definition | `udt_schema` | `udt_name` |
|--------------------------------------------------|---------------|---------------|
| `server/catalog.go:1580` (standalone) | `NULL` (:1640) | `NULL` (:1641) |
| `server/catalog.go:1667` (DuckLake mode) | `NULL` (:1727) | `NULL` (:1728) |
| `server/sessionmeta/sessionmeta.go:744` (session) | `NULL` (:884) | `c.udt_name` (:885) |

A bare `NULL` column resolves to `INTEGER` in DuckDB's catalog — `DESCRIBE` reports it as `INTEGER`, and that is the type a client sees over the wire. Any client that compares `udt_schema` to a string therefore fails, because the string literal gets coerced toward INT32 rather than the column being coerced toward text.

Metabase's Postgres driver does exactly that. Its column-sync query ([`src/metabase/driver/postgres.clj:339`](https://github.com/metabase/metabase/blob/v0.63.2/src/metabase/driver/postgres.clj#L339)) schema-qualifies enum types with:

```sql
CASE WHEN c.udt_schema IN ('public', 'pg_catalog')
     THEN format('%s', c.udt_name)
     ELSE format('"%s"."%s"', c.udt_schema, c.udt_name)
END AS "database-type"
```

which comes back as:

```
ERROR: rpc error: code = Unknown desc = Conversion Error: Could not convert string 'public' to INT32

LINE 1: SELECT c.column_name AS name, CASE WHEN c.udt_schema IN ('public', 'pg_catalog') THEN COALESCE(c.udt_name::"varchar...
                                                                 ^
```

The caret is on the `'public'` literal in the `udt_schema` `IN` list.

(The `COALESCE(...::"varchar", '')` in the echoed statement is the transpiler's own `format('%s', …)` rewrite from `transpiler/transform/functions_compat.go:109`, not what the client sent — noting it so the echo isn't mistaken for a client-side oddity.)

## Impact

Metabase issues one `describe-fields` statement per schema covering every table at once, so a single failure means **zero columns sync for the entire database**. Tables show up with row counts, but every question against them fails with `Table 'X' has no Fields associated with it`. The database looks connected and half-populated rather than broken, which makes it hard to diagnose from the client side.

More generally this hits any client that filters or joins on `udt_schema` — a common pattern for resolving user-defined and enum types.

## Reproduction

Client side: point Metabase (v1.63.2 / OSS v0.63.2, Postgres driver) at a duckgres endpoint, add it as a database, and let sync run. Field sync fails for every table; the error above appears in the Metabase logs from `metabase.sync.util`.

Minimal, engine-side — an INTEGER-typed `udt_schema` reproduces the error text and caret position exactly (DuckDB 1.5.5):

```sql
CREATE TABLE cols AS SELECT 'x' AS column_name, NULL AS udt_schema;
DESCRIBE cols;  -- udt_schema INTEGER
SELECT c.column_name FROM cols c WHERE c.udt_schema IN ('public','pg_catalog');
-- Conversion Error: Could not convert string 'public' to INT32
```

One thing I could not pin down from outside: a plain DuckDB **view** over `NULL AS udt_schema` keeps the column as `SQLNULL` at runtime and tolerates the comparison, even though `DESCRIBE` reports `INTEGER`. The failure needs the column to be genuinely INTEGER-typed by the time the predicate binds. So the type is hardening somewhere in the duckgres path — worker dispatch, the compat-view rebind, or the pgwire type resolution — and it would be worth confirming where before fixing, in case other compat columns are affected the same way. `DESCRIBE main.information_schema_columns_compat` on a live session should show it.

## Notes on the fix

The narrow fix is a typed NULL in all three definitions:

```sql
NULL::VARCHAR AS udt_catalog,
NULL::VARCHAR AS udt_schema,
```

The idiom is already used elsewhere in the same files — `CAST(NULL AS VARCHAR) AS type_udt_name` at `server/catalog.go:1905`, `NULL::INTEGER AS cache_size` at `server/sessionmeta/sessionmeta.go:731` — so not sure if this was intentional or unintentional difference for `udt_catalog` and `udt_schema`.

Two additional items you're there:

1. **Might be worth an audit of the other bare `NULL AS <col>` columns in the compat views.** Under the SQL standard, most `information_schema.columns` columns are `sql_identifier` / `character_data`, i.e. text. Every one currently emitted as an untyped `NULL` is a latent version of this bug for any client that filters on it.

2. **`udt_name` diverges between the definitions.** `sessionmeta.go:885` returns the real `c.udt_name`, but both `catalog.go` definitions return `NULL`. Even after the type fix, a client on those paths gets a NULL `udt_name` for every column — so anything deriving a column's type from `udt_name` still comes back empty.

---

Found while investigating a Metabase instance syncing against a hosted PostHog warehouse endpoint. Source references are against `main` as of 2026-07-30; error text and caret position reproduced locally against DuckDB 1.5.5.

issues.title: control-plane: remote drain is unbounded — idle connections can block pod termination indefinitely
issues.body:
## Problem

In remote/k8s mode the control-plane graceful-shutdown drain is **unbounded**: `HandoverDrainTimeout` defaults to `0` for `--worker-backend remote` (`controlplane/control.go:256-268`). On SIGTERM the CP stops accepting new connections and blocks on `cp.wg.Wait()` until **every** existing connection goroutine returns (`control.go:1556-1631`, `:685/687`).

A connection goroutine (`server/conn.go messageLoop`, `:1047-1064`) returns only on client disconnect/EOF, a fatal error, or an idle-timeout read deadline — and `IdleTimeout` defaults to `0` (disabled). The CP never force-closes a live connection (`activeConns` is just a counter, no registry).

**Consequence:** a single **idle but open** client connection keeps a `Terminating` CP pod alive until the pod's k8s `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` (24h in prod) expires and the kubelet SIGKILLs it. So:
- Rolling deploys / scale-down can leave old CP pods lingering for hours.
- A connection still open at the grace wall is SIGKILLed (ungraceful) instead of draining cleanly.

## Why it is currently 0

The 15m default was deliberately removed after an incident where the timeout cut in-flight customer queries at the wall (see the comment at `controlplane/control.go:256-268`). So we cannot simply reinstate a flat hard cap — that reintroduces the original regression.

Note: CLAUDE.md, `main.go` help text, and the README still say "15m default (remote)" — **stale**, the actual remote default is `0`. Docs should be corrected as part of this.

## Possible directions (for discussion)

- Distinguish **idle** connections from connections with **in-flight work** during drain: after some grace, close idle connections (no active query / txn / stream) while continuing to wait on connections that are actively running work. This bounds drain without cutting live queries.
- Wire a sensible default `IdleTimeout` so abandoned idle connections are reaped in steady state (not only at shutdown).
- A drain deadline that only applies to idle connections, leaving active work unbounded.

## Acceptance

- A terminating CP pod cannot be held open indefinitely by idle connections.
- In-flight queries are still NOT cut mid-execution (no regression of the original incident).
- Stale "15m" docs corrected to reflect actual behavior.

Context: surfaced while designing managed-warehouse compute-seconds billing (`docs/billing-compute-seconds-plan.md`), where shutdown/connection-end semantics matter for metering.

issues.title: Small queries should avoid K8s worker cold-start latency
issues.body:
## Context

`docs/design/worker-ttl-pool.md` documents the current remote/K8s worker TTL model and explicitly leaves per-org reserved minimum capacity as future work. Today, small/default queries benefit from hot-idle reuse only when a compatible worker already exists. After an idle gap, the first small query still has to wait for a new worker pod to become query-ready.

## Why this matters

In testing, spawning a worker on an existing node still took roughly 3-5 seconds before the query could run. That delay is not only node provisioning; it includes pod creation/startup, worker process startup, DuckDB extension/bootstrap/warmup, control-plane health-check confirmation, and tenant activation.

That latency is acceptable for cold or large batch work, but it is a poor fit for small/interactive queries where users expect the query path to feel already warm. The current TTL model improves repeated queries, but it does not protect the first small query after all compatible hot-idle workers have expired.

## Desired outcome

Small/default query traffic should have an operator-controlled way to avoid paying cold K8s worker startup latency after ordinary idle gaps, while preserving the existing remote-worker safety properties: one query session per worker, tenant isolation, version-aware reuse, and predictable per-query resources.

## Related

- `docs/design/worker-ttl-pool.md`
- Remote/K8s spawn-on-demand + hot-idle worker model

issues.title: In-memory (plain CREATE SECRET) user secrets linger across sessions on a reused worker
issues.body:
## Problem

Found while writing a customer-runnable test script for #752 against mw-prod-us: a plain (in-memory) `CREATE SECRET` issued in session A is still visible in session B whenever B reuses the same hot-idle worker — empirically reproduced on a prod duckling. Since hot-idle reuse spans **users of the same org**, user A's in-memory secret (with live credential material) is readable by user B via `duckdb_secrets()` and usable by scope match.

This is pre-existing behavior, **not** a #752 regression: DuckDB secrets are instance-global, and the #752 session-start hygiene wipe deliberately clears only *persistent-storage* secrets, because the system catalog secrets (`ducklake_s3`, `iceberg_sigv4`, `iceberg_oauth`) are in-memory and must survive. Before #752 the same lingering applied to persistent secrets too (worse); the in-memory half of the gap remains.

## Reproduce

```
psql ... -c "CREATE SECRET t1 (TYPE s3, KEY_ID 'x', SECRET 'y')"
psql ... -c "SELECT name FROM duckdb_secrets() WHERE name='t1'"   # new session, reused worker → t1
```

## Proposed fix

Extend `wipeUserPersistentSecrets` (duckdbservice/user_secrets.go) into a full user-secret wipe at session create: drop **all** secrets — any storage — whose name is not reserved (`usersecrets.IsReservedName` covers the system set + `__default_*`/`duckgres_*` prefixes). The reserved-name guard already exists and is already load-bearing for CREATE interception; reusing it here keeps one source of truth. Same one-session-per-worker precondition assertion applies.

Caveat to check: unnamed user secrets get DuckDB default names (`__default_s3`), which collide with the reserved *prefix* — wiping them is correct (they're user-created), so the wipe predicate should be "not a *system* secret name" rather than `IsReservedName` verbatim; may need to split the reserved set (system names vs reserved-for-create prefixes).

The e2e `persistent_user_secret_isolation` assertion in `tests/e2e-mw-dev/harness.sh` should gain a temp-secret leg (user A `CREATE SECRET`; user B must not see it).

issues.title: ToolsAgent V3, @n8n/n8n-nodes-langchain.agent fail
issues.body:
### Bug Description

When a chat session's history contains a turn that was produced via a tool call, the next turn in that same session fails at the AI Agent node (ToolsAgent V3, @n8n/n8n-nodes-langchain.agent) with:

NodeOperationError: messages.0: user messages must have non-empty content

Postgres Chat Memory's own loadMemoryVariables output for the same execution shows the prior turn's Human/AI content is fully intact and non-empty at that point. The corruption happens later, inside ToolsAgent V3's own prompt-assembly step, when it flattens buffered memory into the final Anthropic messages[] array — not in memory storage or retrieval.

### To Reproduce

1. Start a fresh chat session. Ask a question that requires a tool call (e.g. a live-data lookup via an HTTP Request Tool node). It succeeds normally.
2. In the same session_id, ask a second question that also requires a tool call.
3. The second turn fails at the AI Agent node with the error above.

### Expected behavior

The agent loads the prior turn from memory and assembles a valid messages[] array for the new request, the same as it does for any session where the prior turn was answered without a tool call.

### Debug Info

Evidence from two real executions in the same production session, ~9 minutes apart, same session_id, same question text:

Execution A (no prior history, fresh session): succeeds.
Execution B (prior history = Execution A's tool-call-derived turn): fails.

Postgres Chat Memory's loadMemoryVariables output for Execution B — non-empty:
{"id":[...,"HumanMessage"],"kwargs":{"data":{"content":"What's today's day-ahead electricity price..."}}}
{"id":[...,"AIMessage"],"kwargs":{"data":{"content":"**Right now (2026-09-26...**..."}}}

The Anthropic Chat Model node's resolved input for the same turn — the equivalent prior-turn slot renders as an empty Human:/AI: placeholder, which reaches the Anthropic API as messages[0] with no content and gets rejected.

Ruled out:
- Storage shape mismatch: stored memory rows are well-formed JSON with non-empty content matching loadMemoryVariables' output.
- A second writer to the memory table exists in our setup (an internal routing service), but live row shapes are 100% consistent with one shape, and this execution's loadMemoryVariables output was already correct before the failure — so the second writer isn't the cause.

Happy to provide the full resolved JSON (redacted) for the AI Agent node's input/output on the failing execution.

### Operating System

Debian 13 (trixie)

### n8n Version

2.39.8

### Node.js Version

v26.7.0

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Execution mode

main (default)

self hosted

issues.title: deactivated workflows keep running — schedule registrations are never cleaned up
issues.body:
<!-- Please follow the template below. Skip the questions that are not relevant to you. -->

## Describe the problem/error/question

**Schedule Trigger registrations are not cleaned up. A single Schedule Trigger fires more than once per scheduled time, and a registration survives deactivating the workflow — a workflow with `active: false` continues to execute on schedule, indefinitely.**

The workflow record itself saves correctly (verified through the public API), so this is not a persistence problem. The evidence below suggests each activation adds a schedule registration while deactivating removes at most one, leaving the remainder firing.

### Evidence

One workflow, one Schedule Trigger set to `triggerAtHour: 6`, `timezone: Etc/UTC`. Activated
`2026-09-22T06:21:26Z`. Three executions followed, all `mode: trigger` (none user-started):

```
id        startedAt (UTC)       mode      status    workflow state at the time
2735222   2026-09-23 06:00:42   trigger   success   active
2735225   2026-09-23 06:00:56   trigger   success   active
2755546   2026-09-24 06:00:56   trigger   success   INACTIVE
```

Two things to note:

1. **2026-09-23 double-fired** — two executions 14 seconds apart from a single once-daily Schedule Trigger, on the very first scheduled day after activation.
2. **The workflow was deactivated at `2026-09-23T08:06:37Z` and still fired the next morning.** The `:56` registration survived deactivation; the `:42` one did not. The second-offset is preserved exactly across days, which is what suggests these are two distinct registrations rather than a retry.

Workflow state confirmed through the API immediately after the 2026-09-24 execution:

```
active:     false
isArchived: false
updatedAt:  2026-09-23T08:06:37.179Z     (unchanged since the deactivation)
```

So the record says inactive, has said so for 22 hours, and the schedule fired anyway.

### Archiving does not stop a schedule either

Separately, we found that archiving a workflow does not stop its Schedule Trigger. The workflow disappears from the workflow list but keeps firing. This is easy to be caught out by, because archiving reads as a "stop" action and the workflow is no longer visible to check.

**Deleting the workflow outright is the only way we found to actually stop a running job.**
Neither deactivating nor archiving does it.

### What appears to create the duplicate registration

The duplicate appears after **updating an existing workflow by re-importing over it** —
importing a workflow file into a workflow that already exists, rather than creating a new one.
The previously registered schedule is not replaced, so the workflow ends up carrying both the
old and the new registration and fires once per registration.

### What we expected

- One Schedule Trigger fires once per scheduled time.
- Deactivating a workflow removes all of its schedule registrations.
- Archiving a workflow stops it from running.

### Impact

Both behaviours are dangerous for a workflow with external side effects.

Our workflow authenticates to a production API and writes to a shared spreadsheet. The 2026-09-24 execution — the one that ran while deactivated — minted a production access token, read the spreadsheet and parsed 18 rows before stopping. It happened to write nothing only because there was no outstanding work that morning. Had there been, a workflow we had explicitly deactivated would have performed production writes on real customer accounts.

The duplicate fire has the same shape: without mitigation, every scheduled run's side effects happen twice.

We have had to build our own idempotency and kill-switch logic inside the workflow to make scheduled execution safe — a once-per-day lock using `$getWorkflowStaticData`, plus a time-window check and a manual enable flag in a Code node, because Code node edits are the only control we found that reliably takes effect. The once-per-day lock is the only reason the 2026-09-23 double fire was harmless: execution `2735225` was stopped after 2 nodes.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Create a workflow with a single Schedule Trigger at a specific hour and minute, plus one node that records the time.
2. Activate it. Let it fire on schedule.
3. Edit the workflow by **importing a workflow file over it** (update the existing workflow rather than creating a new one), then activate again.
4. Check the executions list filtered to that workflow at the next scheduled time — observe more than one execution, seconds apart, all `mode: trigger`.
5. Deactivate the workflow. Confirm `active: false` via `GET /api/v1/workflows/{id}`.
6. Wait for the next scheduled time.

Observed at step 6: a new execution appears, `mode: trigger`, while the workflow is inactive. Deleting the workflow is the only thing that stops it.

For the archiving variant: activate a scheduled workflow, confirm it fires, archive it, wait for the next scheduled time. Observed: it still fires.

### What we ruled out

- **Not a persistence problem.** `active` and `updatedAt` both update correctly on deactivate, confirmed through `GET /api/v1/workflows/{id}`.
- **Not duplicate workflows.** The instance has three workflows in total, verified through the API. No second copy exists on a similar schedule.
- **Not user-triggered.** Every execution above reports `mode: trigger`.
- **Not the durable scheduler.** That feature does not exist in this version.

## What is the error message (if any)?

**None.** Every operation reports success. The duplicate and the post-deactivation executions are all green. Nothing in the UI distinguishes them from a legitimate run — the executions list shows a normal successful execution for a workflow that the same UI shows as inactive.

The only way we found any of this was by querying the executions API and comparing timestamps against the deactivation time.

## Please share your workflow/screenshots/recording

The behaviour does not appear specific to our workflow — any Schedule Trigger should reproduce it.
A minimal example:

```json
{
  "nodes": [
    {
      "parameters": { "rule": { "interval": [ { "triggerAtHour": 6 } ] } },
      "id": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
      "name": "Schedule Trigger",
      "type": "n8n-nodes-base.scheduleTrigger",
      "typeVersion": 1.2,
      "position": [0, 0]
    },
    {
      "parameters": { "mode": "runOnceForAllItems", "jsCode": "return [{ json: { ranAt: new Date().toISOString() } }];" },
      "id": "22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222",
      "name": "Code",
      "type": "n8n-nodes-base.code",
      "typeVersion": 2,
      "position": [200, 0]
    }
  ],
  "connections": {
    "Schedule Trigger": { "main": [ [ { "node": "Code", "type": "main", "index": 0 } ] ] }
  },
  "settings": { "executionOrder": "v1", "timezone": "Etc/UTC" }
}
```

Our real workflow is not included because it holds production credentials in a Code node. It is otherwise an ordinary linear workflow: Schedule Trigger → Code → HTTP Request nodes.

## Share the output returned by the last node

All three executions ran correctly. The problem is that two of them should never have started.

Node-level detail:

```
2735222  2026-09-23 06:00:42 -> 06:00:47   10 nodes, full chain          (active)
2735225  2026-09-23 06:00:56 -> 06:00:56    2 nodes, stopped by our own
                                            once-per-day guard           (active)
2755546  2026-09-24 06:00:56 -> 06:00:58   10 nodes, full chain,
                                            minted a production token
                                            and read external data       (INACTIVE)
```

issues.title: Queue mode: workflow static data is not reloaded for new executions since #37701 ($getWorkflowStaticData is empty on every run)
issues.body:
### Bug Description

In queue mode, `$getWorkflowStaticData('global')` returns an empty object at the start of every new trigger execution. What a run writes is saved to `workflow_entity.staticData`, but the next run never loads it, so a workflow that keeps a cursor or counter in static data starts from zero every time. Regular (main process) mode is not affected.

**Cause.** #37701 (commit 53ecf6b6be, "Do not persist an execution when preExecute throws") changed `WorkflowRunner.run()` to

```ts
const shouldReloadStaticData = Boolean(existingExecution && loadStaticData);
```

and passes `shouldReloadStaticData` to `enqueueExecution()` where it used to pass `loadStaticData`. For a new execution `existingExecution` is undefined, so the job is enqueued with `loadStaticData: false`.

`prepareNewExecution()` now loads the static data into `data.workflowData.staticData`, but the execution is persisted through `toWorkflowSnapshot()`, which keeps only `id, name, nodes, connections, settings, nodeGroups`. On the worker, `JobProcessor.processJob()` takes `staticData` from `execution.workflowData` and reads the database only `if (loadStaticData)`, so every new execution starts with no static data.

Before #37701 the runner passed `loadStaticData` straight through, and 2.37.7 behaves correctly. `master` has the same code as 2.40.6 as of 2026-09-25.

Possible fixes: pass `loadStaticData` to `enqueueExecution()` for new executions as before, or keep `staticData` in the persisted workflow snapshot.

Workaround: keep cursors and counters in a Data Table instead of workflow static data.

### To Reproduce

1. Run n8n 2.40.6 in queue mode (`EXECUTIONS_MODE=queue`, one worker, PostgreSQL, Redis).
2. Create a workflow: a Schedule Trigger (every minute) connected to a Code node with:
   ```js
   const s = $getWorkflowStaticData('global')
   const before = s.count || 0
   s.count = before + 1
   return [{ json: { before, after: s.count } }]
   ```
3. Activate the workflow and let it run three times.
4. Open the three executions: `before` is 0 in every one, while the workflow's stored static data reads `{"global":{"count":1}}`.

### Expected behavior

`before` is 0, then 1, then 2: each run sees what the previous run saved, as it did in 2.37.7 and still does in main mode.

issues.title: Self-hosted sandbox runner: Security and production recommendations
issues.body:
# Security

The `compose.yml` file recommended at https://docs.n8n.io/deploy/host-n8n/install-options/install-using-docker-compose and used by the `get.n8n.io` script runs the `sandbox-runner-1` container using `privileged: true` and Docker-in-Docker. This essentially gives it root access to the host machine.

The [one-line setup page](https://docs.n8n.io/deploy/host-n8n/install-options/one-line-setup) does not mention that this is a security risk at all. It says:

> this setup uses n8n's own bundled sandbox, which is a good fit for trying things out, but for production, n8n currently recommends Daytona instead.

but has no mention of security risks.

The security checklist on the [install using Docker Compose page](https://docs.n8n.io/deploy/host-n8n/install-options/install-using-docker-compose) touches on it somewhat:

> sandbox-runner-1 (privileged: true, Docker-in-Docker) is never exposed to the public internet. Treat it as equivalent to root on the host.

but I'd go even further and state that **nothing else** should be running on the same system.

# Production

The documentation says that Daytona is recommended in production, but it doesn't say whether that's because there's fundamental differences in a production setup such that it's literally not possible without Daytona, or just because Daytona is easier to set up.

People that self-host tend to not want to use remotely-hosted services - that's the whole reason they're self hosting! That could be for a number of reasons, for example data sovereignty, security, running on an air-gapped system, avoiding vendor lock-in, using local AI models, etc. The docs should be clearer about production use cases for these types of users. 

Is running the bundled sandbox in a dedicated, isolated VM (i.e. only the sandbox running on the VM, nothing else) sufficient for production? If so, maybe this should be a recommended configuration in the [set up AI assistant](https://docs.n8n.io/deploy/host-n8n/configure-n8n/set-up-ai-assistant) docs.

I think it'd be good to have three headings:
1. Self-hosted development: The current all-in-one compose.yml
2. Self-hosted production: Whatever is suitable. Maybe a separate VM for the sandbox? 
3. Remotely-hosted production: Daytona

issues.title: [DOCS-REQUEST] - Document the new "Create Extension" option for Postgres PGVector Store
issues.body:
**Source PR:** https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/pull/33446
**Related GitHub issue:** https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/issues/15739
**Related community post:** https://community.n8n.io/t/postgres-pgvector-store-got-created/151319

**Target docs page:** [Postgres PGVector Store](https://docs.n8n.io/integrations/builtin/cluster-nodes/root-nodes/n8n-nodes-langchain.vectorstorepgvector/) (n8n-docs repo)

## What changed

PR #33446 adds a new **Create Extension** boolean option (under **Options**, default `false`) to the Postgres PGVector Store node, for the Insert, Load, and Retrieve (incl. Retrieve-as-Tool) operations.

Previously, the node always ran `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector` when initializing, which requires Postgres **superuser** privileges. This broke the node for non-admin database users, even when the `vector` extension was already installed by an administrator.

## Behavior change to call out in the docs

- **Default (`Create Extension` off):** the node no longer tries to create the `vector` extension automatically. It still creates the destination table if needed.
- **`Create Extension` on:** restores the previous behavior — the node runs `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector` (schema-qualified if a custom extension schema is configured) before creating the table. Requires database superuser privileges.

## Suggested doc additions

1. Add a new entry to the **Options** section of the node docs page:

   > **Create Extension**
   > Whether to create the `pgvector` extension if it does not exist. Off by default. Requires database superuser privileges. Enable this only if you have superuser access and the extension isn't already installed; otherwise leave it off and have a database administrator install the `vector` extension ahead of time.

2. Add a short note/callout near the top of the page (or in a "Notes"/"Troubleshooting" section) explaining that non-superuser database roles should leave **Create Extension** disabled, and that this is the fix for the previously reported "Because vector isn't a trusted extension, only members of ... are allowed to use CREATE EXTENSION vector" error.

3. If the docs page has a changelog/version note convention, mention this option was added to address GitHub issue [#15739](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/issues/15739).

issues.title: [Feature]: Support persistence-specific annotations on the chart-managed PVC
issues.body:
### Is your feature request related to a problem?

The chart-managed PersistentVolumeClaim only receives `commonAnnotations`. This prevents adding annotations that should apply exclusively to persistent storage.

For GitOps deployments, annotations such as `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options: Prune=false,Delete=false` or `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep` must not be applied globally to Deployments, Services, Secrets, or other chart resources.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Add `persistence.annotations` and apply it to the chart-managed PVC.

The implementation should:

- Preserve the existing `commonAnnotations` behavior for backward compatibility.
- Merge `persistence.annotations` with `commonAnnotations` on the PVC.
- Give `persistence.annotations` precedence when the same key is present in both maps.
- Add the new field to `values.schema.json` and document it in `values.yaml`.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

- Using `commonAnnotations`, which incorrectly applies storage-specific lifecycle behavior to every chart resource.
- Creating the PVC separately and configuring `persistence.existingClaim`.
- Maintaining a wrapper chart solely to create the PVC.

### Feature Category

Storage and persistence

issues.title: hooks.json commands don't quote ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, breaking hooks on Windows when the user path has spaces
issues.body:
## Description

The `command` values in `hooks/hooks.json` reference `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` without wrapping the path in quotes, e.g.:

```json
"command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/session-start.sh"
```

On Windows, plugin installs live under the user's profile directory (`C:\Users\<username>\.claude\plugins\...`). Any username containing a space (e.g. `C:\Users\First Last\`) produces a `CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` value with a space in it. Because the command string isn't quoted, the shell that executes it splits the command line on that space, so it tries to run a truncated path as the executable and passes the rest as an argument.

This affects every hook entry in the file (`SessionStart`, all `PreToolUse` entries, and `PostToolUse`), since they all follow the same unquoted pattern.

## Error

Reproduced the exact failure mode locally by invoking an unquoted path with a space via `cmd.exe /c`:

```
'C:\Users\First' is not recognized as an internal or external command,
operable program or batch file.
```

(`C:\Users\First Last\...\hooks\session-start.sh` gets split into executable `C:\Users\First` and argument `Last\...\hooks\session-start.sh`.)

## Cause

`hooks/hooks.json` interpolates `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` directly into the `command` string without quotes:

```json
"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/session-start.sh"
```

Any path containing a space breaks the command line when the shell parses it. This is expected to hit most Windows users, since Windows commonly uses the full display name (which often contains a space, e.g. "First Last") as the profile folder name.

## Proposed fix

Wrap every `command` value in double quotes, e.g.:

```json
"command": "\"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/session-start.sh\""
```

applied consistently to all six `command` entries in `hooks/hooks.json` (`SessionStart`, the five `PreToolUse` matchers, and `PostToolUse`).

## Environment

- OS: Windows 11
- Plugin: n8n-skills (n8n-io/skills), version 1.2.0

issues.title: get-node.sh reads wrong get_node_types params (ids/name vs nodeIds/nodeId) — per-node hook warnings silently dead
issues.body:
## Summary

`hooks/pre-tool-use/get-node.sh` extracts node names from `.tool_input.ids[].name`, but the current n8n MCP `get_node_types` tool passes `.tool_input.nodeIds[].nodeId`. Both the array key (`ids` → `nodeIds`) and the field (`name` → `nodeId`) drifted. As a result `NODE_NAMES` is always empty and **every per-node high-risk warning is silently dead**: Set, Code, Merge, splitInBatches, DateTime, dataTable. Only the generic once-per-session `node-config` reminder still fires.

This affects **all harnesses** (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) since they run the same script.

## Impact

The node-specific warnings are the highest-value part of the hook — they catch the Set/Code/Merge antipatterns at the moment of node lookup. They have been non-functional wherever the installed n8n MCP uses the `nodeIds`/`nodeId` param shape.

## Repro

Current live `get_node_types` schema: `{ nodeIds: [{ nodeId: "n8n-nodes-base.code", ... }] }`.

Feeding the hook that real shape vs. the shape it reads:

| Input to get-node.sh | `[Code node detected in this lookup]` emitted? |
|---|---|
| `{"tool_input":{"nodeIds":[{"nodeId":"n8n-nodes-base.code"}]}}` (real) | **no** |
| `{"tool_input":{"ids":[{"name":"n8n-nodes-base.code"}]}}` (what the hook expects) | yes |

Only the generic `Before configuring nodes:` reminder appears for the real shape.

## Proposed fix

Read both shapes defensively so it survives past/future param drift:

```bash
NODE_NAMES="$(echo "${INPUT}" | jq -r '
  (.tool_input.nodeIds // .tool_input.ids // []) |
  map(if type == "object" then (.nodeId // .name) else . end) |
  .[]
' 2>/dev/null)"
```

## Notes

- Found while testing the OpenCode plugin (#39): the plugin bridge was relaying this hook faithfully; the hook itself was broken upstream.
- The PostToolUse `validate-workflow.sh` node detection is unaffected (it correctly detected a Set node in the same session).

issues.title: PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook matchers can never fire under Codex — connector tools are named `_get_node_types`, not `mcp__*__get_node_types`
issues.body:
### Summary

Every hook matcher in `hooks/hooks.json` is anchored to Claude Code's MCP tool-naming convention:

```json
"matcher": "^mcp__.*__get_node_types$"
```

Codex does not reach n8n through a local MCP server. It uses a ChatGPT **connector**, and the connector's tools are exposed to the model under a bare, unprefixed name with a leading underscore. Those names cannot match an `^mcp__` anchored pattern, so **no PreToolUse or PostToolUse hook in this plugin can ever fire under Codex.**

This is separate from #46. #46 is about the *payload* shape (`ids[].name` vs `nodeIds[].nodeId`) once a hook has fired; this issue is that under Codex the hook never fires at all. Fixing #46 alone leaves Codex with no hooks.

### Evidence

Tool names as actually invoked, aggregated from 396 local Codex session transcripts (`~/.codex/sessions/**/*.jsonl`, `payload.type == "custom_tool_call" | "function_call"`):

```
  88  _get_execution
  86  _get_workflow_details
  51  _get_node_types
  47  _validate_workflow
  43  _publish_workflow
  29  _update_workflow
  25  _test_workflow
  20  _search_nodes
  15  _execute_workflow
  14  _prepare_test_pin_data
  14  _archive_workflow
  11  _create_workflow_from_code
  10  _search_workflows
   8  _unpublish_workflow
```

Not one carries an `mcp__` prefix. The connector is also visible in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[apps.connector_<id>.tools."n8n_execute_workflow"]
approval_mode = "approve"
```

Firing rate since the Codex plugin was installed (2026-07-19): **13 distinct sessions called `_get_node_types`; the hook produced output in 0 of them.** The check is the presence of the generic reminder string `"Before configuring nodes: invoke the n8n-node-configuration"` anywhere in the session transcript. Codex does register and trust the hooks — `~/.codex/config.toml` carries `trusted_hash` entries for `n8n-skills-windows@personal:hooks/hooks.json:pre_tool_use:0..5` — they simply never match.

### Suggested fix

Widen each matcher to accept both harnesses' naming, preserving the existing anchoring:

```diff
-"matcher": "^mcp__.*__get_node_types$"
+"matcher": "^(mcp__.*__)?_?get_node_types$"
```

Applied to all seven matchers. I have been running this locally against both harnesses and it matches `mcp__<server>__get_node_types` (Claude Code), `_get_node_types` (Codex), and a bare `get_node_types`, without matching unrelated tools.

### One thing I could not determine

Hook stdin is not persisted to Codex transcripts, so I could not verify that Codex populates `.session_id` in the hook input JSON. If it uses a different field name, `_emit.sh` and `get-node.sh` would still exit early at their `[ -z "${SESSION_ID}" ] && exit 0` guard even after the matcher is widened. Worth checking alongside this fix, since both would present identically as "hooks never fire."

### Environment

- n8n-skills 1.2.0
- Codex CLI 0.152.0, Windows 11
- Claude Code 2.1.258 (matchers work correctly there — this issue is Codex-specific)

issues.title: Hooks fail with exit 127 when CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT contains spaces (Claude desktop app, macOS)
issues.body:
## What happens

In the Claude desktop app on macOS, every hook shipped by `n8n-skills` fails before running:

```
/bin/sh: /Users/<user>/Library/Application: No such file or directory
exit code 127
```

The plugin root resolves under `~/Library/Application Support/...`, and `hooks/hooks.json` builds the command in shell form without quotes:

```json
"command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/session-start.sh"
```

The shell splits the path at the space, so the script never starts.

## Impact

- `SessionStart` never injects `using-n8n-skills-official`, on startup, resume, clear or compact.
- None of the `PreToolUse` warnings fire. In three long sessions we measured 31/31, 39/39 and 65/65 failed hook calls on `update_workflow`, `create_workflow_from_code`, `test_workflow` and the others.

The failures are non-blocking, so nothing tells the user that the safety net is off.

## Fix

The Claude Code hooks reference asks for quoted placeholders in shell form, or exec form with `args`:

```json
"command": "\"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}\"/hooks/session-start.sh"
```

or

```json
"command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/session-start.sh",
"args": []
```

The same change applies to every entry in `hooks/hooks.json` (plugin version 1.1.0). Related, but a different environment: #40.

issues.title: n8n-agents-official/SKILL.md points at files that live in other skills — installers can't fetch it
issues.body:
## Summary

`skills/n8n-agents-official/SKILL.md` references two files under `references/` that aren't in its own directory:

- `references/AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md` — the file lives at `skills/n8n-binary-and-data-official/references/AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md`
- `references/COMMS_NODES.md` — the file lives at `skills/n8n-node-configuration-official/references/COMMS_NODES.md`

Tools that build a skill package from the `references/...`, `templates/...` tokens inside `SKILL.md` can't assemble this one, so they refuse to install it.

## Steps to reproduce

```bash
hermes skills tap add n8n-io/skills
hermes skills install n8n-io/skills/skills/n8n-agents-official
```

Result:

```
Fetching: n8n-io/skills/skills/n8n-agents-official
Error: Could not fetch 'n8n-io/skills/skills/n8n-agents-official' from any source.
```

I walked the repo tree at commit `046c330c9308bbfc54ceab1adbe3d8fc6bebc8fa` (2026-08-18): `SKILL.md` lists 10 referenced files, but `skills/n8n-agents-official/references/` has only 8 (`CHAT_AGENT_PATTERNS.md`, `HUMAN_REVIEW.md`, `MEMORY.md`, `RAG.md`, `STRUCTURED_OUTPUT.md`, `SUBWORKFLOW_AS_TOOL.md`, `SYSTEM_PROMPT.md`, `TOOLS.md`) plus an `examples/` dir. `AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md` and `COMMS_NODES.md` are missing.

The offending lines:

```markdown
84:  Full pattern in `n8n-binary-and-data-official` `references/AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md`
88:  Pattern in `n8n-binary-and-data-official` `references/AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md`
214: See `n8n-node-configuration-official` `references/COMMS_NODES.md` "Block Kit messages"
```

## Expected behavior

`hermes skills install n8n-io/skills/skills/n8n-agents-official` (and equivalent Agent Skills installers, e.g. `npx skills add n8n-io/skills`) installs the skill complete, with all files it references.

## Actual behavior

The install fails. The two tokens are read as local files of `n8n-agents-official`, the check fails, and the installer gives up. The other skills in the repo install fine, so the problem is specific to this one.

## Proposed fix

Option A, simplest: copy `AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md` and `COMMS_NODES.md` into `skills/n8n-agents-official/references/` (tweak the text so it doesn't duplicate the sibling skills' guidance).

Option B, if the cross-skill pointers are intentional: reword the three lines so the path doesn't start with an allowed support-dir token. Use a full markdown link instead:

```markdown
Full pattern in [`n8n-binary-and-data-official/references/AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md`](n8n-binary-and-data-official/references/AGENT_TOOL_BINARY.md)
```

Paths that start with `references/`, `templates/`, `scripts/`, `assets/` or `examples/` get treated as local skill files by agentskills.io tooling. Prefixing with the sibling skill path removes the ambiguity.

Worth grepping the other skills for the same pattern: cross-skill `references/...` tokens pointing outside the owning directory.

## Verification

After the fix:

```bash
hermes skills install n8n-io/skills/skills/n8n-agents-official   # should succeed
```

issues.title: Codex Desktop on Windows cannot reliably execute the shipped shell hooks
issues.body:
## Environment

* Windows 11
* Codex Desktop / Codex mode in the ChatGPT desktop app
* Codex `0.145.0`
* `n8n-skills@n8n-io` `1.0.2`
* Upstream commit `eb18fc3ab3e2820c748c2d84386fb5496efc1516`

Claude Code works with the same plugin. Codex Desktop on Windows does not reliably execute the shipped hooks.

## Reproduction

1. Add the `n8n-io/skills` marketplace in Codex.
2. Install `n8n-skills@n8n-io`.
3. Restart Codex and approve the plugin hooks.
4. Start a new Codex session.

The plugin points Codex at `hooks/hooks.json`, where the hook commands directly invoke `.sh` files.

The SessionStart hook also relies on Bash and uses `jq`, with `python3` as a fallback, to produce its JSON output.

On a normal Windows Codex Desktop installation, these assumptions are not portable. The shell scripts may fail to execute or may open through a file association instead. Bash, `jq`, or `python3` may also be unavailable.

When this happens:

* SessionStart does not load `using-n8n-skills-official`;
* PreToolUse and PostToolUse reminders do not run;
* the plugin appears installed but does not behave as documented.

## Expected

The README says the plugin works in both Codex CLI and Codex mode in the ChatGPT desktop app.

It should therefore work on Windows Codex Desktop without requiring users to install or configure Bash, `jq`, or `python3`.

## Temporary solution I am using

I currently apply a local Windows compatibility repair that:

* adds a PowerShell launcher for the hooks;
* routes the Windows hook commands through that launcher instead of invoking `.sh` files directly;
* adds a Node.js JSON fallback so hook output does not depend only on `jq` or `python3`;
* preserves the existing skill and hook behaviour.

This works as a temporary compatibility layer, but it has to be reapplied or revalidated when the plugin updates.

## Suggested fix

Please consider either:

* host-neutral Node.js hook entry points; or
* explicit Windows PowerShell and POSIX shell launchers selected by platform.

Windows Codex Desktop coverage should include:

* startup;
* resume;
* clear;
* compact;
* PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks;
* paths containing spaces;
* systems without `jq` or `python3`.

If Windows Codex Desktop is not intended to be supported, the README should narrow that claim and installation should fail visibly instead of installing hooks that cannot run.

## Problem

This repo has no tags, no GitHub releases, and no version-pinning mechanism. Skills here (e.g. `n8n-workflow-lifecycle-official`) reference MCP tool names matching whatever `main` currently targets, the latest n8n release. Anyone running an older, still-supported self-hosted n8n version gets a skill calling tools their instance doesn't have.

Concrete example: PR #34347 (merged 2026-07-29, first shipped n8n@2.34.0) renamed five MCP tool names at once (`prepare_test_pin_data`→`prepare_workflow_pin_data`, `search_executions`→`search_workflow_executions`, `get_execution`→`get_workflow_execution`, `list_tags`→`list_workflow_tags`, `get_sdk_reference`→`get_workflow_sdk_reference`). PR #45 synced this repo to the new names. Anyone on n8n 2.31.5-2.33.7 pulling `main` today gets a skill referencing tools that don't exist on their server. Commit `046c330c9308bbfc54ceab1adbe3d8fc6bebc8fa` (the state just before #45) still has the old names, as a manual workaround.

Also worth fixing here: the README documents a `#v1.2.0` tag-pin syntax for OpenCode users, but no `v1.2.0` tag, or any tag, exists in this repo, so that instruction doesn't work today.

## Ask

A way to consume a version of these skills pinned to a specific n8n release, e.g. tagging a release alongside each "adopt n8n X.Y MCP surface" sync PR (like #45, #32), or at minimum a compatibility note/table mapping commits to the n8n version they were verified against.

## Reported by

A self-hosted Enterprise customer hit this evaluating `n8n-workflow-lifecycle-official` against n8n 2.31.5, via n8n Support.

issues.title: Security review: n8n-debugging skill contains persistence-oriented guidance
issues.body:
## Problem
The `n8n-debugging` skill from the official `n8n-io/skills` repo is being blocked by Hermes' skill security scan as **DANGEROUS**.

The main concern is a **persistence-oriented instruction** in a reference file: the scan flagged a step that tells the user to note an issue number (existing or newly filed) in workflow files. That crosses from debugging guidance into embedding external ticket metadata into workflow artifacts, which is hard to audit and can create unwanted self-referential persistence.

The scan also flagged a couple of medium-severity execution findings around upstream data stripping. Those are more like standard debugging advice, but the persistence instruction is the one that looks materially unsafe.

## Why this matters
- It encourages persisting ticket/issue metadata inside operational workflow artifacts.
- It makes the workflow harder to review and reason about later.
- It creates a pattern where debugging notes can become embedded state.
- Hermes' security scanner is treating it as a blocking issue.

## What I expected
A debugging skill should stay focused on diagnosis and repair without instructions that persist issue numbers or other ticket metadata into workflow files or generated artifacts.

## Suggested fix
- Remove or rewrite any instruction that tells the user to store issue numbers in workflow files or related operational artifacts.
- Keep the skill limited to observation, diagnosis, and reversible changes.
- If the skill needs to reference a bug tracker, do it in a separate non-persistent note or an external report, not inside the workflow artifact itself.

## Context
I hit this while reviewing the skill for use in a Hermes-based n8n setup. I did not force-install it because the security scan blocked it.
